items.title: Temple of Heaven
items.desc: Far south east of Qianmen and the Tiananmen Square and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Not only a beautiful sight, but also surrounded by a vast public park popular with local residents practicing tai chi, dancing, and so on in the mornings and on weekends. Home to many ancient trees, this is also the gree
items.price: For entry to the park and historical sights (like the temple): ¥35 (¥30 in winter half year); park only: ¥15 (¥10 in winter half year)

items.title: Longtan Park
items.desc: Park with lake, boats for hire, teahouses and a restaurant, children's playground, pavilions, a bird market and a lot of dragons. There is also a climbing wall and a roller skating area in the park.

items.title: Ming Dynasty City Wall Site Park
items.alt: 明城墙遗址公园 Míng Chéngqiáng Yízhǐ Gōngyuán
items.desc: Beijing's city wall was built around 1435. It stretched for 23.5km with one part running where Metro Line Two is now (inner city wall) and one part running where the southern part of Ring Road Two is now. Since 1949 (and especially around 1965), most was torn down to make room for Ring Road Two, Metro Line Two and Tian
items.price: Park is free; ¥10 for the tower

items.title: Beijing Amusement Park
items.desc: Beijing's first amusement park. Quite large with many rides. Most rides are ok. The location in and around a lake is fine, but the landscaping is not very inspired and the atmosphere is a bit boring, especially on days with few visitors.

items.title: Shrine of Yuan Chonghuan
items.alt: 袁崇焕祠和墓; Yuánchónghuàn Cíhémù
items.desc: Yuan Chonghuan (1584-1630) was a famous hero and prominent marshal of the Ming Dynasty.

items.title: Fire God Temple
items.desc: Newly renovated temple.

items.title: Beijing Museum of Natural History
items.desc: Large museum with a lot of information on nature, but some of the exhibitions are a bit old fashioned. Exhibitions cover paleontology, zoology, animal behavior, botany, the original of human beings, dinosaurs, aquarium, the human body, cells, skeletons and an interactive park.

items.title: Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall
items.desc: Museum with a large model of the city, historical pictures from the city and also other exhibitions with relation to the layout and structure of Beijing.

items.title: Red Gate Gallery
items.desc: Red Gate was founded in 1991 by Australian Brian Wallace. The gallery exhibits work by contemporary Chinese artists reflecting China's changing society in relation to daily life, gender, population, and the environment. The media are traditional Chinese painting, collage, lithographs and oil painting.

items.title: Qianmen
items.desc: Built in 1419 as the front gate of the inner city wall. Was originally only used by the emperor on his way to Tiantan. Now it houses exhibits with photos and models of the old city.

items.title: Chongwen south of Ring Road Two
items.desc: Explore the part of Chongwen stretching down beneath Ring Road Two. Here is an area, which seems to have been forgotten by the city planners. Hutongs and small shops, restaurants and businesses are thriving here seemingly undisturbed by the rapid development elsewhere in Beijing. It is a nice place for a walk into the

items.title: Chongwen Workers' Palace
items.desc: Theater specialised in kung fu plays. Also art and culture exhibitions as well as a cinema in the same building.

items.title: Chongwen's hutongs
items.desc: Take a walk in the rapidly disappearing small streets of the Chongwen hutongs. The present situation (March 2009) is that the area between Qianmen Dajie (前门大街) and the newly established Qianmen East Street (前门东路) is not accessible due to the ungoing renovation, which can be expected to transform the area to a touristy

items.title: Party Life
items.desc: Karaoke.

items.title: Hong Qiao (Pearl) Market
items.desc: Not far from the Temple of Heaven. Worth visiting for the state-run silk market but more especially for the pearl market in the building opposite. The top two floors of this market are filled with jewelry, and this may be the best place in China to buy pearls, coral, turquoise, amber and other semi-precious stones. The

items.title: New World Shopping Centre
items.desc: Five storied shopping mall.

items.title: Qianmen Carpet Co.
items.desc: Claims to be the first established antique carpet dealer in China. Sells antique carpets as well as reproductions.

items.title: Chongwenmen Food Market
items.desc: Traditional indoor food market with lots of small stalls with all kind of fresh food ingredients. This is the oldest remaining traditional food market in Beijing and worth a visit, also if you are not buying anything.

items.title: Soshow
items.desc: Entertainment Shopping Center for the young, rich and modern Beijingers.

items.title: Hongqiao Wet Food Wholesale Market
items.alt: 红桥水产批发市场; Hóngqiáoshuǐchǎnpīfāshìchǎng
items.desc: Raw food whole sale market specialising in sea food but also with other.

items.title: The small streets north of Hong Qiao Market
items.desc: In these streets there are a number of small and inexpensive restaurants.

items.title: Old Beijing Noodle King
items.desc: Specialised in hand made noodles, but also other courses available. Bustling and authentic atmosphere.

items.title: Hengxingde Dining-hall
items.desc: Sichuan Cuisine.

items.title: Beijing Gongdelin Vegetarian Restaurant
items.alt: 北京功德林素菜饭庄; Běijīnggōngdélínsùcàifànzhuāng
items.desc: Established in 1922. Traditional Buddhist vegetarian restaurant specialised in courses imitating meet but based on toufu, mushrooms etc.

items.title: Yunteng Restaurant
items.desc: Yunnan cuisine, specialising in mushroom dishes. Located in the Yunnan provincial office building, and the food is as expected very Yunnan. The restaurant tries to look like a Yunnan rain forest, but does not really succeed, and the service level is not impressive, but the food is excellent.
items.price: Expect ¥50-75 each person, more if you want some of the fancier mushrooms

items.title: Ye Shan Jun Wild Fungus House
items.desc: Hot pot specialising in mushrooms.

items.title: Mala Youhuo
items.desc: Sichuan cuisine. Very popular restaurant.

items.title: Bianyifang
items.desc: The oldest roast duck restaurant in Beijing with a history dating back to 1416. Many branches throughout the city including three in Chongwen.

items.title: Chongwenmen Wai Dajie branch
items.desc: The flagship branch of the chain.

items.title: Daijiacun Restaurant
items.desc: Dai Minority cuisine. The restaurant is decorated in classical Dai style. Dai traditional dancing and singing now and then.

items.title: Yushan Restaurant
items.desc: Imperial cuisine.

items.title: Capital M
items.desc: Capital M is a modern Australian/European style restaurant. It provides cuisine and ambiance of a high standard. It overlooks part of Tiananmen Square and several colourful Chinese buildings which are illuminated at night. By Australian standards it provides excellent value.

items.title: Maxim's de Paris
items.desc: Traditional French cuisine and one of the first foreign restaurants to open in Beijing.

items.title: Chairman Mao Memorial Hall
items.desc: The body of the founder of the People's Republic of China, Mao Zedong, has been preserved (against his own wishes) and is on display in here. Expect huge, but moving, queues. No bags, cameras or water bottles are allowed inside and must be dropped off (for a fee) at the bag-check building across the road to the east (m
items.hours: Open Tu-Su, 8AM to noon (but note it is sometimes closed without notice)

items.title: Monument to the People's Heroes
items.desc: A cenotaph with round-the-clock honor guard commemorating the PRC's veterans and war dead. Illuminated at night. Usually blocked off unless there is an important ceremony or visitors, but even then only those participating can go to the base of the cenotaph. However, you can usually get close enough to take pictures.

items.title: Tian'anmen Gate
items.alt: 天安门; Gate of Heavenly Peace
items.desc: Tian'anmen Gate, and its large portrait of Chairman Mao, dominates the northern end of the square. This was originally the main gate into the Imperial City, and is the only one of the four gates that still survives. Pass beneath the gate to head north toward the Forbidden City. It costs nothing to pass through, but on

items.title: Forbidden City
items.alt: 故宫 Gù Gōng, also known as the Palace Museum
items.desc: China's last imperial palace occupies the centre of Beijing. All visitors must enter through the Meridian Gate from Tiananmen Square to the south; exit is via the north or east gates. Get there at opening time if you want to walk through the vast and spectacular courtyards in relative peace. This is truly the spot to a
items.hours: April 1st-October 31st: 8:30AM-5PM. November 1st-March 31st: 8:30AM-4:30PM. Closed on Mondays out of summer season.

items.title: Yonghegong
items.alt: 雍和宮; Yōnghégōng; also known as Lama Temple or Palace of Peace
items.desc: The temple was built by Chinese emperors who harbored a deep fascination for the Tibetan (Tantric) version of Buddhism. Over the years, many Tibetan and Mongolian monks lived and taught here, and some are still in residence today. The temple is famous for its 18m (60 ft) statue of Maitreya Buddha carved from a single p

items.title: Zhihua Temple
items.alt: 智化寺; Zhìhuàsì; also known as Temple of Wisdom Attained
items.desc: Buddhist temple built in 1443. One of the largest, oldest and best preserved wooden structures in Beijing. Houses the Ancient Music Center, which now and then gives concerts played by monks according to ancient traditions. Also houses the Beijing Cultural Exchange Museum. Recently renovated.

items.title: Tongjiao Temple
items.alt: 通教寺; Tōngjiāosì; also known as Temple of Authoritative Teaching
items.desc: Originally used by eunuchs but now actively used by nuns.

items.title: Confucius Temple
items.desc: The temple was built in 1302 and honors Confucius (孔子; Kǒngzi; 551-479 BC) who was one of China's greatest thinkers, still with significant influence on all aspects of daily life. The pavilions along either side have displays about Confucius and the history of Confucianism The courtyard is a pleasant place to relax or

items.title: Imperial Academy
items.desc: The academy was the highest level college and location of examinations for the civil service in Imperial China. Very much related to the neighbouring Confucius Temple in that the studies and exams were conducted in the Confucian tradition. Displays documenting the history of the imperial exams system and the lives of s

items.title: Beijing Police Museum
items.alt: 北京警察博物馆; Běijīng Jǐngchá Bówùguǎn
items.desc: Large museum on police history.

items.title: Imperial City Art Museum
items.desc: The Imperial City was the Manchu city that surrounded the Forbidden City during the Qing dynasty. The museum's centrepiece is a scale model of the Forbidden & Imperial Cities. There are also displays on lifestyle, costumes, arts & crafts of the Qing imperial city. Occasionally hosts special exhibits that cost extra.

items.title: National Art Museum of China
items.alt: 中国美术馆, Zhōngguó Měishù Guǎn
items.desc: China's premier art museum with over 35,000sqm of exhibition space in 21 halls on four stories. Collection exhibits both ancient and contemporary work, with some Western art as well. Should become easier to reach once planned subway stop opens.
items.price: Free, but only 4,000 tickets available until 4PM daily

items.title: National Museum of China
items.alt: 中国国家博物馆 Zhōngguó Guójiā Bówùguǎn
items.desc: A huge museum containing the ancient and recent history of the Chinese nation. Modern history exhibit focuses on the successes of the Communist party (and obviously not the negatives). Most exhibits have short English explanations.
items.price: Free; foreign visitors must show their passport

items.title: The Poly Museum
items.desc: Small art museum specialising in bringing Chinese artifacts home to China from abroad. Main exhibitions cover ancient bronze art, ancient stone carvings and Buddha statues.

items.title: Mao Dun Former Residence
items.desc: Mao Dun (1896-1981) was a famous revolutionary writer. His former residence including personal effects and writings can be seen here.

items.title: Dadu Museum of Art
items.desc: ''Beijing Dadu Museum of Art'', a high-profile institution in the public interest, was built with the strong support and assistance of the Beijing Culture & Art Foundation and China Oil Painting Society. The museum has opened to the public since 2013 after 04 years of construction. Covering an area of 11,000 square met
items.hours: Opening Time 09:30 am - 17:30 pm ( After 16:00 No Entering and it's Closed in Mondays)
items.price: 老人、军人、及残疾人士请携带相关证件，凭证件免票。 学生请携带学生证，购买学生票

items.title: CourtYard Gallery
items.desc: Founded in 1996. Exhibits emerging and mid-career artists working in a wide range of media.

items.title: onemoon
items.desc: Chinese artist working in a range of media.

items.title: Wan Fung Art Gallery
items.desc: Worth a peek if you're in the area. Housed in a side building in the courtyard of the Imperial Archives, which you can't go in, but is quite impressive. The courtyard itself is a quiet corner in an otherwise crowded area of the city.

items.title: Zhongshan Park
items.desc: Beautifully landscaped park with lots of trees and bamboo. Paddle boats for rent on the moat of the Forbidden City. Also an indoor playground for children, and bumper cars.

items.title: Changpu River Park
items.desc: Narrow strip of landscaped park along a small stream. Begins in the east near the Beijing hotel and runs almost to Tian'anmen Gate.

items.title: Ditan Park
items.alt: 地坛公园; Dìtán Gōngyuán; also known as Temple of Earth
items.desc: Park with a lot of cypresses and also a small amusement park area.

items.title: Liuyin Park
items.desc: Park showing what rural China looks like. Also contains children's playground and a tea house.

items.title: Qingnianhu Park
items.desc: The park contains basketball, croquet, golf, electric boats, paddleboards and an amusement zone. Waterland contains a large pool with waterslides.
items.hours: Park: summer 6AM-10PM, winter 6AM-9PM; Water world: summer 9AM-10PM, winter closed

items.title: Drum and Bell Towers
items.desc: The Drum Tower was built in 1272 and moved to a new location in 1800. The Bell Tower was built around 1700. Originally, the towers were used to play music and later on to tell Beijingers the time. Now they house a 63-ton ancient copper bell and a number of ancient/replica drums. Free guides start tours at specific time
items.price: Drum tower: ¥20; Bell tower ¥15; Ticket for both ¥30; half-price for students

items.title: Legation Quarter
items.desc: The legation quarter was once, as its name suggests, home to Beijing's many foreign diplomatic missions. During the 1900 Boxer Rebellion, the diplomats and Chinese Christians who sought their protection held out here until a 55-day siege was broken by foreign forces coming over the city walls. The embassies have since

items.title: Ancient Observatory
items.desc: The observatory, built in 1442, has been open to the public since 1983. Ancient star maps and instruments to watch stars can be seen here. Displays on the history of Chinese astronomy, and several large astronomical instruments set on top of an old watchtower of the city walls.

items.title: Chaonei No. 81
items.desc: This abandoned, overgrown Baroque Revival complex, dating to the early 20th century, has acquired an international reputation as the best-known allegedly haunted house in China. According to residents of the nearby hutongs, even the Red Guards moved out after a few days, supposedly scared off by the ghost of a Kuominta

items.title: Beijing Seven-Color Light Children's Theater
items.alt: 北京七色光儿童剧院; Běijīngqīsèguāngértóngjùyuàn
items.desc: As the name would suggest, shows for children

items.title: Capital Theater
items.desc: This theater is used by a number of different theater groups, including Beijing People's Art Theater. Performances include both contemporary and classical Chinese plays.

items.title: Central Academy of Drama Theater
items.alt: 中央戏剧学院实验小剧场; Zhōngyāngxìjùxuéyuànshíyànxiǎojùchǎng
items.desc: Performances include both plays and dance.

items.title: Central Experimental Drama Theater
items.desc: Both Chinese and foreign plays and both classical and experimental.

items.title: Chang'an Grand Theater
items.desc: Traditional Chinese performances with focus on Beijing Opera. Also has a shop with paintings and folk handicrafts.

items.title: China Children's Art Theater
items.desc: Established in 1956. Stages children's plays.

items.title: Poly Theatre
items.desc: Large theater holding 1,428 seats, eight balcony boxes and two VIP boxes. Chinese, classical music, opera and ballet performances are staged here by both Chinese and international artist groups. The [Beijing Music Festival http://www.bmf.org.cn] is also held here.

items.title: Universal Theater
items.desc: Acrobatic show performed by China Acrobatic Troupe. The theater itself is less impressive than the show.

items.title: Goldsail Concert Hall
items.desc: Small concert hall without speakers. Suitable for chamber music also.

items.title: Culture Yard
items.desc: Explore Chinese culture through various workshops. Culture Yard is a foreign-run cultural centre in the heart of Beijing that offers language courses as well as cultural workshops, which focus on introducing Chinese culture to the international community, and foreign culture to the local community. Culture Yard hosts f

items.title: Hutong Cuisine Cooking School
items.desc: A few places around Nanluoguxiang now offer Chinese cooking classes. One such place, Hutong Cuisine, is run by an English-speaking chef in a small hutong home. Classes are small. Reservations are necessary. Optional market tours are also conducted before cooking classes commence.

items.title: New China Children's Store
items.alt: 新中国儿童用品商店; Xīnzhōngguóértóngyòngpǐnshāngdiàn
items.desc: Play center for children where the kids can catch goldfish, play in the gigantic sandpit or other. They also sell all kind of gear for children.

items.title: Natooke
items.desc: Bicycle shop for hire, purchases and upgrades owned by a champion bike acrobat.

items.title: Wangfujing
items.desc: Beijing's most famous shopping street, nowadays with mostly the same international brands and modern malls you will find anywhere else in the world. The street is pedestrianised for several blocks, making it pleasant to walk around. Several large malls in the area such as Oriental Plaza (see below) and Sun Dong An plaz

items.title: The Malls at Oriental Plaza
items.alt: 东方新天地 Dōngfāng Xīn Tiāndì
items.desc: At one time this was the largest mall in Asia. Modern shopping mall is expensive but provides you with a lot of buying opportunities from diamonds, to real (affordable) DVD's, (international) music CD's and food. You can find lots of brands in Oriental Plaza, from high-end to low. Besides shopping, you also can eat her

items.title: Nanluoguxiang
items.alt: 南锣鼓巷; Nánluógǔxiàng; some partly translated signs say 'South Luogu Alley'
items.desc: This restored hutong, just east of Drum Tower and Houhai, is lined with boutiques and small shops. Not the place for bargains, but this is where to come for unique and distinct gifts including T-shirts, pottery, jewellery, etc.

items.title: NagQu
items.desc: A small shop selling handcrafted bags, scarfs and pottery made with natural materials.

items.title: Poetry Cafe
items.desc: A beautiful cafe with soul as its name "Poetry", is operated by a lovely young lady, who enjoy travel and photography, that she successfully gather a group of 'specialists' in those fields; thus, customers can get tonnes of information about travel and photography. Customers can enjoy a view of the Forbidden City over

items.title: Wangfujing Snack Street
items.desc: Many stalls selling Beijing-style snacks, both sweet and savoury.

items.title: Donghuamen Night Market
items.desc: The place to come for exotic snacks such as scorpions, starfish, and silkworm grubs. You can also buy more typical snacks like fried noodles, dumplings, and kebabs. More expensive than a "real" neighbourhood market, but still reasonably priced.

items.title: Oriental Dumpling King
items.desc: Cheap and delicious Dongbei (northeast) style dumplings. This is a chain, one of several around town. Their location in Harbin is recommended in several guidebooks, but if you're not going there you can get the same dumplings in Beijing. A few dozen different kinds, and can be boiled or fried. As with many dumpling pla

items.title: Guijie
items.desc: Beijing's most famous food street is probably Guijie (sometimes called Ghost Street), which runs east-west along Dongzhimen Nei Dajie from Jiaodaokou Dong Dajie to Dongzhimen Lijiaomen Bridge on the Second Ring Road, Dongcheng District. Red lanterns, traditional courtyards, hundreds of restaurants along the street. Eat

items.title: Huajiayiyuan
items.desc: One of the largest tourist traps. Tasteless food in lovely plates though. Housed in a series of interconnected courtyards. Not as much for people who like Chinese food; rather those who like taking pictures of food. Try places where you see locals waiting on benches to be seated instead.

items.title: Donglaishun
items.desc: This king of Beijing hotpot has been around since the 19th century. Founded by the Hui (ethnic Muslims), Donglaishun serves halal cuts of top-quality lamb and beef. Also serves cooked-by-chef dishes, including traditional Beijing sweets.

items.title: Wangfujing branch
items.desc: Subway: Line 1 to Wangfujing

items.title: Yuxin Sichuan Restaurant
items.desc: One of the contenders in the ongoing competition for Beijing's best Sichuanese, Yuxin delivers on authenticity, flavor, and service. It's always busy, and always good.

(长安大剧院，建国门内大街7号 ''Chángān Dàjùyuàn, Jiànguómén Nèidàjiē Qī hào''). ''(Take the subway Lines 1 or 2 to Jianguomen, take Exit A, and walk west)''. Try their location in the Chang'an Grand Theatre for a calmer setting decorated in a traditional style, with alcoves divided by bamboo screens.

items.title: Yuxiang Renjia
items.desc: Delicious Sichuan food. If you want to try Sichuan but are a little afraid of the spiciness, this place is a good choice: It's still spicy, but not as mouth-numbing as some other places. Reasonable prices, and a faux rural-village decor. There are a dozen locations around town.

items.title: Mr Shi's Dumplings
items.desc: Mr. Shi’s Dumplings restaurant is different from other dumpling hot spots in Beijing, in that although it is good, it totally caters to foreigners.

items.title: Underground Restaurant
items.desc: Romantic Italian-Chinese fusion in an underground hideaway.

items.title: Vineyard Cafe
items.desc: Great place for Western-style breakfast and brunch in a restored hutong home. Also great European/fusion dishes, including some vegetarian options. A good dessert choice is the chocolate brownie with ice cream.

items.title: Xiao Xin's Cafe
items.desc: One of the original cafes along this hutong, and now has many imitators. Great coffee and desserts, although the rest of the food is not particularly special.

items.title: Pebbles Courtyard
items.desc: This restaurant's Mexican offerings are authentic, and the soft-shelled tacos are excellent. It's a nice location to spend a laid-back evening.

items.title: Jardin de Jade
items.desc: A great restaurant for Cantonese and Shanghainese food.

items.title: Dadong Duck Restaurant
items.alt: 大董烤鸭店 Dàdŏng Kăoyā Diàn
items.desc: Considered by some to be the best Peking duck in the city, this upscale restaurant also delivers on a nice atmosphere. Reservations suggested. full/half Peking duck is ¥240/120 with extra ¥8 for condiments. Meal is served with free hot water, small soup, light fruits and black sesame for dessert.
items.price: sea cucumber ¥200-600, lobster ¥200+, steamed humphead wrasse with green shallot ¥2000y, +10% service charge

items.title: Dongsi Shitiao branch
items.desc: This is the newer and more impressive of Dadong's branches.

items.title: Brian McKenna @ The Courtyard
items.desc: The Courtyard overlooks the moat surrounding the south-east corner of the wall of the Forbidden City. At night, the wall and tower are illuminated which gives a sense of being in old Peking. The cuisine is modern international fusion food. After the original Courtyard closed in 2012, McKenna and the original owner reop
items.price: ¥588/person for six-course tasting menu; wine extra

items.title: Saveurs de Coree
items.desc: Korean food in a fancy setting. Can be expensive, but special set menus are a good deal.

items.title: 12SQM
items.desc: Very small bar/café that takes its name from its original floor space (website claims it's the smallest in Beijing, although it ''has'' expanded to 45sqm since)

items.title: Guitar Bar
items.desc: Very small bar with standard drink and Italian food. Guitar jam most nights.

items.title: Hutong Bar
items.desc: Small bar serving tea and beer.

items.title: Jianghu Bar
items.desc: Simple live music venue.

items.title: alba
items.desc: Bar serving signature cocktails, mixed drinks, rums and whiskeys.

items.title: Mao Live House
items.desc: Live rock music venue. The stage is great, the sound system is okay and the concert room and furniture are very basic.

items.title: The Pool Bar
items.desc: Yes, they do have a pool table (and also foosball).

items.title: Reef Bar
items.desc: Basic bar.

items.title: Salud
items.alt: 老伍酒吧 Lǎowǔ Jiǔbā; e.a.t
items.desc: A Spanish-style tapas bar. Blues jam every Thursday, 9pm. ¥20 for 0.5l Tsingtao.

items.title: Tree House
items.desc: Small and quiet pub/café, one of the few to be open also in the morning. Evening events now and then.

items.title: Great Leap Brewing I 大跃啤酒
items.desc: Quite possibly the most difficult bar to find in Beijing. Although it's in the center of everything it's nestled so snugly inside a residential neighborhood that it's nearly impossible for first-timers to locate. It's one of Beijing's first (if not the first) real microbrewery. Founded by a few American guys and one's

items.title: Pass By Bar
items.desc: Cool bar in the heart of Nanluoguxiang, serves beer and food, with open-air upstairs to look out over the hutongs. Lots of great posters to admire.

items.title: Hot Cat Club
items.alt: 北京热力猫音乐俱乐部
items.desc: Going to this live music venue at Fangjia 46 is a like having a band play in your living room at a house party. There's room to dance in front of the makeshift stage and couches to escape a set you're not that into. With great imported beers, friendly staff, and all their shows being free, it's a great place to check o

items.title: Ball House
items.desc: Bar with pool and foosball. Frequented by local artists.

items.title: Bed Bar
items.desc: Relaxed bar with a lot of rugs and pillows.

items.title: Drum and Bell
items.desc: Best part of this bar is the comfortable rooftop patio (especially if you can score a table with couches) that overlooks the Bell Tower and the square (which at night is clear of tour buses and used by locals playing badminton).

items.title: Jiangjin Bar
items.desc: The cocktails are not good, but the live folk music jam is great.

items.title: Zen Bar
items.desc: Very small and quiet bar hidden away in a hutong. Nice simple surroundings including a lot of Buddhas.

items.title: Earl Bar
items.desc: Very basic bar with local DJs.

items.title: Mao Mao Chong Bar
items.desc: This relaxed hutong pub serves reasonably priced international beers, wines and stellar cocktails. The walls are decorated with art and t-shirts for sale by the bar's owners, a husband-wife team who also cook up some of the city's best pizzas. Just east of Nanluoguxiang, Mao Mao Chong is the perfect escape from Beijing
items.price: Cheaper than most bars in Beijing

items.title: Minty
items.desc: Neighborhood bar with live folk music now and then.

items.title: Star Live
items.desc: Medium sized live rock music venue specialising in death metal. Staging both Chinese and international bands.

items.title: Tango
items.desc: Big club with a vast dance floor, a chillout lounge and KTV. Features big-name DJs.

items.title: Tantra
items.desc: Buddha temple themed cocktail lounge with English speaking crew and house music.

items.title: Yugong Yishan
items.desc: The cream of Beijing's nascent rock scene can be enjoyed at this modern and tastefully presented venue.
items.price: ¥20 and up for drinks, shows are between ¥30 and ¥80

items.title: Paddy O'Shea's
items.desc: Beijing's original Irish Sports Pub with daily events

items.title: Modernista
items.desc: Modernista is a European-inspired cafe, restaurant and bar in the heart of Beijing traditional hutongs. They also showcase what they say is "the best of Beijing´s live music, performances, art and cultural events".

items.title: The Distillery by Capital Spirits
items.desc: Capital Spirits claims to be the world’s first bar dedicated to baijiu and craft liquor. The serve baijiu, craft Chinese beers, lesser-known fine spirits from around the world, and specialty baijiu cocktails.

items.title: Ming Dynasty Imperial tombs
items.desc: A part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Imperial Tombs of the Ming and Qing Dynasties". This is the final resting place of 13 of the 16 emperors the Ming Dynasty. The largest and most impressive of them is Changling (长陵), the tomb of Emperor Yongle (永乐皇帝), the 3rd emperor of the Ming Dynasty. Another notable one is D

items.title: China Aviation Museum
items.alt: 中国民航博物馆; Zhōngguó Mínháng Bówùguǎn
items.desc: A must see for all aviation fans. It is probably better known by the name Datangshan. The museum hosts over 200 exhibits, many of them very rare.
items.price: Entrance to the ground exhibits were free (Oct 2011). There is an entrance fee to the indoor display and hanger ¥20, and an extra ¥10 if you want to board Chairman Mao's plane and another ¥10 to board a DC-8 (Orbis), and ¥10 to sit in a MIG-15

items.title: Dynasty Wax Works Palace
items.desc: Here you can see China's historical and cultural figures in wax.

items.title: Beijing Central Art Gallery
items.desc: Contemporary Chinese paintings and sculptures.

items.title: Open Gallery
items.desc: Contemporary Chinese art.

items.title: Happy Land Arts and Crafts Center
items.desc: The center offers pottery, painting, paper folding, jewelry making and other.

items.title: Tianyi Farm Strawberry Emporium
items.desc: A large strawberry farm in the countryside of Changping. From December to May you can pick your own strawberries for purchase. The strawberries are expensive so remember to pick only the best ones you can find.

items.title: Ban Ruo
items.desc: Buddhist vegetarian restaurant. Try the fake Beijing Duck and other fake meat dishes.

items.title: Kyros Kebab
items.desc: Kebabs and sandwiches.

items.title: Bravo
items.desc: Italian restaurant.

items.title: Obelisco
items.desc: Argentinian restaurants serving great steaks and red wine.

items.title: Haru Teppanyaki and Sushi Bar
items.desc: Sushi is served at the bar while you can have both sushi and teppanyaki in the private rooms. Unusually high level of service here.

items.title: The Pomegranate
items.desc: Sports bar hidden in the hutongs of Shunyi.

items.title: The Cellar Lounge
items.desc: Wine bar with imported red wine and snacks.

items.title: Beihai Park
items.desc: Beihai is a former imperial garden centred on a lake with interesting religious and garden architecture. There's a big island and white pagoda which was built in the 17th century. The giant buildings westward outside are PRC's Ministry of Defence and General Staff, which, to be honest, ruin the scene of the west bank.

items.title: Beijing Zoo and Aquarium
items.alt: 北京动物园 Běijīng Dòngwù Yuán
items.desc: (They do have pandas but displays aren't as good as other places in China, such as the Panda Breeding Centre in Chengdu, Sichuan Province). The animals are kept in very small cages in which they pace to and fro in sheer restlessness and desperation. The lion and tiger building is particularly disappointing, housing a c
items.hours: Zoo 1 Apr-31 Oct 7:30AM-6PM; Zoo 1 Nov-31 Mar 7:30AM-5PM; Aquarium 1 Apr-31 Oct 9AM-5:30PM; Aquarium 1 Nov-31 Mar 9AM-5PM

items.title: Jingshan Park
items.desc: Jingshan is another former imperial garden with some imperial garden architecture. A popular next stop after leaving the Forbidden City from the north gate, this 23-hectare (57-acre) park is built around Jingshan, the artificial hill created with the soil dug to build the Forbidden City's moat. Literally meaning "Prosp

items.title: White Cloud Temple
items.desc: Taoist temple established in 793. Houses the Chinese Taoist Association and a Taoist Health Clinic.

items.title: Guanghua Temple
items.desc: Buddhist temple used to pray for success in business life.
items.hours: 1st and 15th day of the lunar month 8AM-5PM

items.title: Guangji Temple
items.alt: 广济寺; Guǎngjìsì; also known as Temple of Great Charity
items.desc: Buddhist temple built around 1460. Burned down in 1934 and was rebuilt in 1952 and further renovated in 1972. It is supposed to look as it did originally, but it does not really look old. The temple is functioning as a center for Buddhist thinking and learning and it is also the headquarter of the Chinese Buddhist Asso
items.hours: 8AM-4:30PM but only partly open to the public

items.title: Lidai Diwang Miao
items.alt: 历代帝王庙; Lìdàidìwángmiào; also known as Temple to Emperors of Past Ages
items.desc: Large temple built in 1530 used to sacrifice to past emperors. Opened to the public in 2004 after a decade of renovation. Here can be seen memorial tablets for a large number of past emperors.

items.title: Capital Museum
items.desc: New high profile history and art museum located in an impressing building. Exhibits include the history of Beijing and artifacts from throughout China's history.
items.price: Free, tickets must be reserved three days in advance on the official website

items.title: Prince Gong's Mansion and Garden
items.desc: The mansion displays the life of princes during the Qing dynasty. The garden is packed with Chinese tourists. The mansion stages Peking Opera and magic shows now and then.

items.title: Soong Ching Ling's Former Residence
items.desc: Museum and garden showing the life of Soong Ching Ling (1893-1981). Soong was a politician in the early days of communist China, vice president 1959-1975. She was married to Sun Yat-sen and also related to Chiang Kai-shek.

items.title: Mei Lanfang's Residence
items.alt: 梅兰芳纪念馆; Méilánfāng Jìniànguǎn
items.desc: Museum showing the life of Mei Lanfang (1894-1961). Mei was the greatest star of Peking Opera, acting for more than 50 years, primarily playing female roles. Furniture as well as costumes and other opera stuff are exhibited here.

items.title: Guo Moruo's Former Residence
items.desc: Museum showing the life of Guo Moruo (1892-1978). Guo was an author, poet, historian and government official. His works seems quite dated now, but his former residence is still worth a visit.

items.title: China Science and Technology Museum
items.alt: 中国科技馆; Zhōngguó Kējì Guǎn
items.desc: Educuational museum with the possibility of experimenting yourself. Hall A has short films, Hall B has exhibitions, whereas Hall C is an experimental area primarily for children.
items.price: Hall A and B: ¥30 for each or ¥50 combined, children free; Hall C: ¥10, ¥20 children

items.title: Xu Beihong Museum
items.alt: 徐悲鸿纪念馆; Xúbēihóng Jìniànguǎn
items.desc: Xu Beihong (1895-1953) was one of the first and most influential modern Chinese painters. He used both Chinese and Western techniques and is most famous for traditional painting of running horses. The museum exhibits a large number of his own works as well as his large collection of other artists' works.

items.title: Beijing Lu Xun Museum
items.alt: 北京鲁迅博物馆; Běijīng Lǔxùn Bówùguǎn
items.desc: Lu Xun (1881-1936) was one of the first and most influential modern Chinese writers. He is most famous for "The True Story of Ah Q". The museum consist of Lu Xun's former residence as well as an exhibition hall with exhibits of Lu Xun's personal effects, originals and copies of his works and also exhibits not dirictly

items.title: Deshengmen
items.desc: City gate built in 1437 as part of the city wall, which was torn down in 1969. Now only an archery tower and a barbican is left. The gate houses an ancient coin exhibition and a snack bar.

items.title: Great Hall of the People
items.desc: Seat of China's parliament and venue for important political meetings. While the hall is normally used for meetings for the National People's Congress, there are occasionally classical-music concerts held there.

items.title: Zhongnanhai
items.desc: This former imperial garden centred on two lakes is now the headquarters of China's government and ruling party. The compound is no longer open to the public, but you can take a photo in front of the distinctive south gate and revolutionary slogans fronting West Chang'an Avenue. You can also see the back of the compoun

items.title: Beijing Exhibition Theater
items.alt: 北京展览馆剧场; Běijīng Zhǎnlǎnguǎn Jùchǎng
items.desc: Theater from 1954 with a theater hall with 1,000 seats. The theater is part of a multifunctional building with exhibition, hotel, restaurant and entertainment. Wide range of shows including Chinese plays, Western and Chinese operas and ballets, musicals and rock concerts.

items.title: Beijing Youth Palace
items.desc: Cinemas with Chinese and foreign movies. Also music and dance classes available.

items.title: Ethnic Cultural Palace Theatre
items.alt: 民族文化宫大剧院; Mínzúwénhuàgōng Dàjùyuàn
items.desc: Performances of classical music, ballet, musical, opera, drama plays and movies.

items.title: PLA Song and Dance Theater
items.alt: 解放军歌舞剧院; Jiěfàng Jūngēwǔ Jùyuàn

items.title: Central Conservatory of Music
items.alt: 中央音乐学院; Zhōngyāng Yīnyuèxuéyuàn
items.desc: The main purpose of the conservatory is to educate musicians. Concerts now and then.

items.title: National Centre for the Performing Arts
items.desc: Theater complex with three halls (opera, music and theater) covering almost 12,000m2 and seating a total of 5,452 people. One of the most stunning buildings in Beijing and a must see even if not attending an opera or concert.

items.title: Houhai
items.desc: Take a walk in the Houhai area.

items.title: Beijing Planetarium
items.desc: Here you can watch movement of stars and planets, creation of the solar system, evolution of life, space shuttle simulation and the history of the sun.

items.title: Philippe Active Space Station
items.alt: 菲利普宇宙空间站; Fēilìpǔyǔzhòukōngjiānzhàn
items.desc: Play center for children including ball pool, maze and arts and crafts area.

items.title: Beijing Capital Times Square
items.alt: 首都时代广场; Shǒu​dū​ Shí​dài​ Guǎng​chǎng​
items.desc: Shopping center focusing on international brands.

items.title: Grand Pacific
items.desc: Has a good selection of less expensive brands and attracts primarily younger shoppers. The shopping mall appears bright and clean and it is usually not too crowded. Here you can find makeup, clothes and sports. Restaurants include Bread Talk, DQ, Pizza Hut and Sizzler.

items.title: Joy City
items.desc: This mall opende in 2008 is the largest in Xidan and you can find almost everything here including an enormous cosmetic shop. The building has an impressive glass facade and inside the feel is spacious despite the hords of locals browsing here.

items.title: Xidan Department Store
items.desc: Government owned mall with a history of more than 70 years. It has been redecorated several times over the years but still appears a bit old fashioned. The prices are good though.

items.title: Zhong You Department Store
items.desc: Has a lot of fake brands (mostly clothes). Very affordable if you bargain hard.

items.title: Xizhimen
items.desc: One of the most popular markets for locals is located in '''Xizhimen''', next to the zoo. items.title: Sihuan Mixed Goods Market
items.desc: Raw food whole sale market.

items.title: Beijing Commodity Market
items.desc: 40,000 sqr meter large market offering a wide range of products including fashion, gifts, leather goods and toys.

items.title: Tian Zhao Tian Market
items.desc: Jewelery market.

items.title: Jiumen Xiaochi
items.desc: This traditional place hidden in the hutongs close to Houhai houses ten or so vendors. Before choosing from the many different simple and traditional dishes here, you will have to go to the cashier and add value to the shared charge card. This is a very popular place with locals and can be packed, especially in weekend

items.title: Ri Chang
items.desc: Simple Cantonese restaurant with good food but unimpressive service and decoration.

items.title: Nevertheless Café
items.desc: A cool bar by the side of Houhai Lake.

items.title: Fengyuan Baozipu
items.desc: Cantonese cuisine. Serves simple dishes like baozi, congee, doufu soup. Very busy at lunch.

items.title: Shaguoju
items.desc: Manchurian cuisine. This restaurant has been around for centuries, but surprisingly the service is still good and the prices low despite the increasing popularity. items.title: Koufuju
items.desc: Restaurant specialising in hot pot with a large selection of meat to choose from.

items.title: Charme
items.desc: Cantonese restaurant popular with Hong Kong expats and tourists.

items.title: Qingzhen Xiaochi
items.desc: Simple and cheap Beijing cuisine, eg fried noodles. Busy serving elderly locals who appears to come here almost every day.

items.title: Xi'an Restaurant
items.desc: Xi'an cuisine. Serves halal dishes. This restaurant has a long history, and is said to have been a favorite of Chairman Mao. Specialties include mutton soup and steamed mutton.

items.title: Xidan Chiku
items.desc: Serves Beijing cuisine specialising in chicken wings.

items.title: Ma Bashi Restaurant
items.desc: Busy small restaurant specialising in beef noodles and Xinjiang noodles.

items.title: Jinfuyuan

items.desc: Small restaurant popular with locals. Serves Beijing cuisine, specialising in rice carrerole and rice noodles.

items.title: Kong Yi Ji
items.desc: Traditional Zhejiang cuisine in modern surroundings.

items.title: Raj Indian Restaurant & Bar
items.alt: 拉兹印度餐厅; Lāzī Yìndù Cāntīng
items.desc: Great Indian restaurant in an old building with rooftop views over the area. Serves both traditional and modern Indian dishes, which tastes pretty much like in India.

items.title: Cafe Sambal
items.desc: Traditional authentic Malaysian cuisine and flavours.

items.title: Sichuan Restaurant
items.desc: Sichuan cuisine.

items.title: Hutong Pizza
items.desc: Small courtyard restaurant serving both typical and more sophisticated pizzas. Quite limited selection of beers.

items.title: Kao Rou Ji
items.desc: Halal restaurant specialising in Beijing-style roast lamb/mutton and beef, but best known for the lamb/mutton. This restaurant has been around for more than 100 years and has great views of the lake from the second floor. A favourite of the Prince Regent Zaifeng in the 19th century. In the early 20th century it was one

items.title: House of Poo Restaurant
items.desc: Great but safe destination for families with children who love imagination and grossing out.

items.title: Yuxin Sichuan Restaurant
items.desc: One of the contenders in the ongoing competition for Beijing's best Szechuan cooking, Yuxin delivers on authenticity, flavor, and service. It's always busy, and always good.

items.title: Kao Rou Wan
items.desc: Xinjiang cuisine specialising in roast meats.

items.title: Xiang E Qing
items.desc: Hunan and Hubei cuisine.

items.title: Beijing Ren Grand Restaurant
items.desc: Cantonese cuisine.

items.title: Hui Feng Hot Pot
items.desc: Beijing cuisine specialising in hot pot served in the traditional copper cone pots with coal.

items.title: Hot & Tasty
items.desc: Sichuan cuisine as hot as you will find it in Sichuan.

items.title: Royal Icehouse
items.desc: Beijing cuisine. The restaurant is in the former royal ice house.

items.title: Tong He Ju
items.desc: Shandong cuisine. This restaurant has been around for centuries. It is spacious with large tables.

items.title: Yu Guo Tian Qing
items.desc: Beijing cuisine specialising in dumplings.

items.title: The Woods

items.desc: Serves "exceptional Continental Cuisine with a fashionable twist."

items.title: Await Café
items.desc: A true travellers café, with three floors, meals, drinks and desserts, filled with souvenirs from the four corners of the globe.

items.title: The Gourmet Room
items.desc: Hong Kong cuisine served in courtyard restaurant. Offers a classic 10 course menu.

items.title: Lijia Cai Restaurant
items.desc: Imperial cuisine. This is a small family run restaurant in a hutong. The set menus consist of ten cold dishes and eight hot. The dishes are small and quite simple, but very tasty. There are only three tables in the restaurant, so book in advance.

items.title: Haiqing Heyan
items.desc: Small courtyard restaurant serving French Teppanyaki. There is great views of the lake from the four private rooms. Modern and stylish decor. Reservations are needed.

items.title: Ken de Rouge
items.desc: Modern Chinese cuisine. This is a romantic restaurant with views of the lake.

items.title: The Noble Restaurant/Bar
items.desc: Zhejiang-French fusion restaurant with views of the lake.

items.title: Fu Lin
items.desc: Zhejiang cuisine served ub courtyard restaurant with trees, pond and views of the lake.

items.title: Whampoa Club
items.desc: Serves modern Chinese food based on the old tradtions of Beijing cuisine.

items.title: Temple Kitchen
items.desc: Modern Chinese food.

items.title: Restaurant at 95
items.desc: A modern palace with exquisite style and traditional imperial service. Suitable for small group dining.

items.title: 15 Qianhai Beiyan
items.desc: Both indoor and outdoor seatings and good with of the lake.

items.title: Blue Lotus Club
items.desc: Kitch bar with Chinese live instrumental orchestra in the weekend.

items.title: Cam Rang
items.desc: Quiet Vietnam inspired lounge with large and soft sofas.

items.title: Houhai Paradise
items.desc: Dance club with loud house music and a small dance floor.

items.title: Huxley's
items.desc: Simple bar frequented by both tourists and locals.

items.title: Jiadingfang
items.desc: Large place by the lake with a long list of drink and food. Live music every night, primarily unknown local bands.

items.title: Lotus Blue
items.desc: Bar with live music and Thai food. DJ plays house on Fri and Sat, a Chinese band plays blues on Thurs and an African band plays pop on Sun and Mon.

items.title: Luna Bar
items.desc: Relaxed place with local DJs.

items.title: Rive Gauche
items.desc: Quiet cocktail bar.

items.title: Upsetter's Bar
items.desc: Reggae bar with outdoor seating by the water. One of the few places in Houhai where the theme actually works.
items.price: Cheaper than most places in Houhai

items.title: Dao Club
items.desc: Club playing hip-hop and other retro stuff. Stylish but still relaxed place.

items.title: Cigar Legends Bar
items.desc: Lounges primarily frequented by cigar smokers. First class interior with deep upholstered armchairs.

items.title: Grand View Garden
items.desc: Garden established in the 1980s based on the novel 'The Dream of the Red Mansions'. 125,000 m2 with temples, pavilions and other buildings as well as miniature gardens. Traditional ceremonies performed now and then. The park also has a restaurant.

items.title: Taoranting Park
items.desc: A former hangout for literati, while most other Beijing parks were for imperial families only. The park has a total area of 240,000 m2 with water area accounting for 69,000 m2. The park is a mixture of ancient construction styles and modern park design. It was built in 1952. Taoran Pavilion (one of the four most import

items.title: Niu Street Mosque
items.desc: Famous Mosque build in 996 and the oldest and largest of the mosques in Beijing. Structured as a traditional Chinese palace, but also uses typical Arabic decoration with a lot of red colour. A must see if staying for more than a few days. The Muslim presence in the area is obvious with many Muslim shops and Arabic sign

items.title: Fayuan Temple
items.desc: This Buddhist temple was built in 645 and rebuilt in 1436-1449, which makes it the oldest existing in Beijing. Now, it is the site of the Chinese Buddhist Academy and the exhibition center for Buddhist cultural relics, and is also an important institution training young monks and Buddhism research. The temple covers 6,

items.title: Baoguo Temple
items.desc: Founded in 1103, various uses during the next centuries, almost forgotten after 1949, but now renovated and open to public. There is also an antique market specialised in picture books and calligraphies, including writing tools and paper.

items.title: Museum of Ancient Architecture
items.desc: Museum with a model of Beijing ancient city as well as exhibits of Beijing's ancient architecture.

items.title: Song Tang Zhai Museum of Traditional Chinese Folk Carving
items.alt: 松堂斋民间雕刻博物馆; Sōngtángzhāimínjiāndiāokèbówùguǎn
items.desc: This is a small privately owned museum showing carvings in doors, furniture, other wood and stone.

items.title: Museum of Ancient Pottery Civilization
items.desc: Shows the Chinese history of pottery from Neolithic Age to now.

items.title: Huguang Huiguan Theatre
items.desc: Theatre primarily performing excerpts of traditional Chinese opera. The theatre has been working since the 1830s. The theatre building from 1830 is the oldest and best preserved indoor theatre in Beijing. It is in area with other traditional buildings. Next to the theatre is an opera museum.

items.title: Lao She Teahouse
items.desc: See listing in Drink Section.

items.title: Li Yuan Theatre
items.desc: Plays from the Beijing Opera repertoire. Also exhibitions of opera costumes and other. Tea and snacks available.

items.title: Tianqiao Theatre
items.desc: Theater with a seating capacity of 1,200 with performance of local folk music and dance, talk shows, and international ballet and musicals.

items.title: Tsinghua Chi
items.desc: A spa experience from the famous Qinghua Chi, established in 1905. Great service. Affordable TCM treatments. Try the Ba Guan (Cupping) or acupuncture or opt for simpler manicure and pedicure and Massage.

items.title: Walk the hutongs of Xuanwu District

items.desc: Qianmen Dajie is one of Beijing's oldest commercial streets with a 500 year old history. Now, this street is under reconstruction to bring it back as it was in the 1920s. items.title: Dashilan
items.desc: Dashilan (and surrounding streets) is a shopping area dating back to the Ming dynasty. The name means big fences, which in earlier times were in place in both ends of the street. Everything burned down during the boxer uprising in 1900, but the area has since been reestablished as a shopping area

items.title: Daoxiangcun
items.desc: Famous shop established in 1895. Best known for its wide selection of southern style cakes. More than 20 branches around the city.

items.title: Liubiju
items.desc: Famous shop established in 1530. Sells pickled vegetables.

items.title: Liulichang
items.desc: There is no production here any more, but rather antique stores, selling Chinese painting, handicrafts, and used books. The area was popular back to the Tang dynasty, but the small shops were amalgamated into state-operated units during the 1950s. It was redeveloped as a tourist area after 1979, but has failed to regai

items.title: Beijing Qianxiangyi Silk Store
items.alt: 北京谦祥益丝绸商店; Běijīngqiānxiángyìsīchóushāngdiàn
items.desc: Very large silk store established in 1840. Claims to be the biggest silk professional store in China.

items.title: Tea Street
items.desc: The street has 8 wholesale tea markets and more than 600 tea shops. Tea sets also for sale here.

items.title: Sogo
items.desc: Shopping mall with Japanese and European shops.

items.title: Carrefour
items.desc: French supermarket.

items.title: Lanhuahua Restaurant
items.alt: 兰花花美食村（lán huā huā měi shí cūn
items.desc: Serves Shaanxi cuisine.

items.title: Little Sheep
items.desc: Mongolian hot pot restaurant with branches nationwide and abroad. Richer soup and, therefore, no dipping sauce.

items.title: Tan Yu Tou
items.desc: Primarily serves spicy sichuan hotpot with fish or meat.

items.title: Bhodi-Saki
items.desc: Located just north of Taoranting Park in the south west corner of Beijing, this isolated vegetarian restaurant is situated inside a series of old courtyards that house the restaurant and a small temple.

items.title: Jin Yang Restaurant
items.desc: Jin Yang Restaurant serves Shaanxi cuisine. Four Star Restaurant.

items.title: Quanjude
items.desc: The oldest and most venerable of the roast duck restaurants. Quanjude is slipping these days, but its fame still brings many customers, mostly tourists eager for the classic experience. items.price: Ducks cost ¥199 each and ¥99 for half a duck

items.title: Lao She Teahouse
items.desc: Large tea house from 1988 named after the writer, Lao She. Serves tea and traditional snack. Live performance every night with acrobatics, opera and other traditional art.

items.title: Chen Clan Academy
items.desc: This is very well preserved architecture from the 19th century. It used to belong to a wealthy family by the name of Chen and now houses many articles including ivory sculptures and artistic statues.

items.title: Memorial of the Huangpu Military Academy
items.alt: 黄埔军校旧址 Huáng-pǔ-jūn-xiào-jiù-zhǐ, Huangpu is also spelled Whampoa
items.desc: The original Military Academy was founded in 1924 by Sun Yat-sen, with support from the Chinese Communist Party and the Soviet Union. items.title: Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall
items.desc: Dedicated to the founder of the Republic of China and local hero Dr. Sun Yat-Sen. It was constructed in 1931 and built on the original site of Sun Yat-sen's presidential office on Yuexiu Hill.
items.price: Admission is free for the park and ¥10 to go inside the hall

items.title: Canton Tower
items.desc: It was the tallest structure in China prior to the topping out of Shanghai Tower. It is 595.7 m height and it's now the third tallest tower and the fifth-tallest freestanding structure in the world. It has indoor public observatory at 449 m and outdoor observation deck at 488 m. In additions to the observation decks, t

items.title: Xiguan Residence
items.desc: See the traditional Cantonese architectures from the Qing Dynasty. These houses can be found in Duobao Road (多宝路), Baohua Road (宝华路), Longjin West Road (龙津西路) and Shangxiajiu Road (上下九路). One of the most famous ones is located at 18 Baoyuan North Street (宝源北街18号). They were occupied by the upper class in the old days.

items.title: Guangzhou Traditional Buildings
items.desc: Are slowly disappearing due to the rapid growth in the city. Remaining buildings can be found near Yide Road, Renmin Nan Road and Zhongshan Road. They make great photo spots.

items.title: Shamian Island
items.desc: The buildings and streets of the former British and French concession have been beautifully renovated, creating an oasis of tranquility in an otherwise bustling and hectic metropolis. One of the old structures is '''Our Lady of Lourdes Chapel,''' located at 14 Shamian Street. The architecture reflects the colonial era

items.title: Former Residence of Hong Xiuquan
items.desc: The former home of the quasi-Christian leader of the Taiping Rebellion that resulted in the death of about 20 million people during the late Qing dynasty. items.title: Xiaozhou Village
items.desc: The village is a short taxi ride from University City. Some travelers describe this district as full of historical buildings, fruit orchards and canals and relate that, in recent years, this has become artists' haven. Others report that recent development has obliterated all traces of the village and that the district

items.title: Xiao Bei / Siu Bak
items.desc: Likely Guangzhou's most diverse neighborhood, with banners here written in at least 4 languages: Chinese, English, French and Arabic. You'll find delicious Middle Eastern restaurants before you meander into side streets full of Africans. Even the Chinese salespeople here have thick African accent when they speak Englis

items.title: Shishi Sacred Heart Catholic Cathedral
items.desc: It is one of the oldest church structures in the city, and the largest of its kind of Southern China. It is currently in use for worship.

items.title: Liurong Temple

items.title: IFC Mall
items.desc: Sleek and impressive, this is arguably the most prestigious shopping centre on the island. Here you will find one of the best cinemas with the added bonus that the film will be the English language version (if it is an animation). Go up to the rooftop and you will find yourself in what is technically public open space.

items.title: The Landmark
items.desc: An older shopping centre that has had a recent facelift to incorporate a five-star hotel. For many, it remains a focus for many of the most expensive designer fashion shops in Hong Kong.

items.title: Pedder St and Queen's Rd
items.desc: One of the best locations for jewellery and designer watches at prices that can be up to 35% less than Europe. As always, shop around for the best prices and always buy from reputable dealers to avoid fake goods.

items.title: Pacific Place and Queensway and Admiralty Centre
items.desc: A number of interconnected shopping malls near Admiralty MTR. Pleasant air-conditioned shopping for mid-price to expensive branded goods and restaurants.

items.title: Soho and south of Hollywood Rd area
items.desc: Has a new a trendy shopping area around Staunton and Lower Elgin St with lots of local designers.

items.title: The Lanes
items.desc: Buy silks, fabrics, Chinese dresses, watches, leather bags and many other things here. Despite its prime location close to Central MTR, these narrow streets have a reputation among locals for quality goods at competitive prices.

items.title: Cat Street
items.desc: Probably the best place to buy souvenirs, lots of Mao memorabilia, porcelain, buddha statues and "antiques". Lok Ku Rd, walk down Hollywood Rd towards the west, when you see the Man Mo temple walk down the stairs on the right hand side.

items.title: Dumpling House
items.desc: Great Beijing-style dumplings, avoid going there during lunch hour, because it is packed.

items.title: Good Luck Thai
items.desc: Seating is both indoors and outdoors, very popular on weekends, nice atmosphere.

items.title: Law Fu Kee
items.desc: Popular little restaurant serving congee and noodles.

items.title: Wai Kee Congee Shop
items.desc: A good place to sample some traditional Hong Kong style food.

items.title: XTC Gelato
items.desc: A popular place to get your fix of ice-cream or frozen yoghurt.

items.title: Zhong Guo Song
items.desc: Good Chinese food, without MSG and less oil.

items.title: China Tee Club
items.desc: A colonial gem. A private club that welcomes visitors.

items.title: Lin Heung
items.desc: This is one of the most authentic old world style dim sum restaurants in Hong Kong that uses trolleys to cart its dim sum snacks instead of ordering it using the tick box sheet. Be prepared for a stress induced visit to this restaurant as it is always crowded and you need to work out the system on finding an empty seat

items.title: L16 Cafe and Bar
items.desc: Serves Thai and Italian food, but come for the location - not the food. A rare place to drink and eat outside away from the noise of Central.

items.title: Maxim's Palace
items.desc: One of Hong Kong's most popular dim sum spots, featuring harbour views if you're lucky enough to score a window table. The atmosphere and food are very much in the classical dim sum tradition, a large, noisy hall with waitresses pushing around carts laden with goodies; try the siu mai (燒賣), har gao (蝦餃) and mango puddi

items.title: Pizza Express
items.desc: Has a nice view overlooking the Mid-Levels Escalator.

items.title: Yung Kee Restaurant
items.desc: This is a popular place for Cantonese style Roast Goose and century eggs. Come early and make reservations as they have been known to run out of geese!

items.title: Baci
items.desc: Pizza.

items.title: Beirut
items.desc: Lebanese cuisine is top of the sheet. Lamb or chicken kebab and sisha. Nice decor but the food is a far cry from the real deal (particularly in taste).

items.title: Tokyo Joe
items.desc: Japanese food.

items.title: Fung Shing Restaurant
items.desc: Very local eatery known for its ''dim sum'', which is cheap and good at $10 and up per serving. Open daily from 7:30AM for the dim sum breakfast crowd, but no English menu.

items.title: Al Dente
items.desc: Italian cuisine. Serving large, medium quality dishes not too different from what you would find in an Italian bistro. Their pastas and meat dishes are better than their pizzas. Often full.

items.title: Ayuthaiya
items.desc: Thai cuisine. Serving quite authentic food in a stylish, dark environment.

items.title: Brunch Club
items.desc: Neighbourhood-style Western coffee shop (pre-Starbucks style) specialising in brunch and breakfast, although dinner is also served. Customers are provided with a wide range of newspapers and magazines in English and Chinese. Clientele is mainly expatriate.

items.title: Double Happiness Cafe
items.desc: Shanghai cuisine. Nice and simple little restaurant serving authentic Shanghainese dishes. Prices reflects that this is in the centre of Soho and comparable food can be found much cheaper elsewhere.

items.title: Jashan
items.desc: Indian cuisine. Serves great curries and perfect naan. The lunch buffet is good value.

items.title: Life Restaurant
items.desc: Organic, vegetarian food.

items.title: Oola
items.desc: Away from the crowds in Soho, but worth the extra walk. International menu in a comfortable environment. Serves as both a place to eat or drink. Drinks are expensive.

items.title: La Pampa
items.desc: Argentinian.

items.title: The Peak Lookout
items.desc: Serving a range of international cuisine such as naan bread, Hainan chicken, and steaks in a 19th century heritage building. Also has a pleasant garden patio.

items.title: Percy Bakery
items.desc: A high quality bakery. Take away and delivery service only.

items.title: Bistro Bouchon
items.desc: French bistro focusing on steaks.

items.title: Chez Patrick
items.desc: An excellent, Parisian-style French restaurant. The proprietor, Patrick, has a delightful obsession with foie gras which extends to creative dishes such as foie gras ice cream served as a first course.

items.title: Chilli Fagara
items.desc: Sichuan cuisine. Great spicy dishes including the favourites you will find in Sichuan Province. This restaurants ambitions appear to go further than just making the food as the mainland original implying that some might be disappointed. Somewhat overpriced but still good.

items.title: Yung Kee Restaurant
items.desc: Established in 1942, this restaurant has enjoyed unparalleled success and was once named in the "Top Fifteen Restaurants in the World" by Fortune Magazine. Previously a humble BBQ house serving its renowned roast goose, it has evolved into a world famous Cantonese restaurant. Dim sum is also served at lunch-time. Be pr

items.title: HAHAClub
items.desc: For cheaper booze, you can try here.

items.title: Works
items.desc: A good place for tourists to start on the gay bar-scene. Popular with expats and tourists alike, it is easily accessible in Central. Friday and Saturday are the most popular nights but do not expect many drinkers to arrive much before 11PM.

items.title: The Globe
items.desc: Excellent beer pub, also has good menu aimed at western taste buds. It is also one of the few places that has Typhoon T8 on tap, a locally produced cask ale.

items.title: Liquid Lounge
items.desc: Chic and classy bar serving food.

items.title: Propaganda
items.desc: Famous gay club. Tends to get going after Works has faded.

items.title: Ocean Terminal
items.desc: Visitors can not help but be impressed by the spectacle and majesty of 40,000 tonne cruise liners parked in the heart of the city. Begin your walk by inspecting the historic clock tower, which is all that remains of a railway station that once took colonial officials back to London via the Trans-Siberian railway.

items.title: Avenue of Stars
items.desc: Look down to see where so many local film stars have pawed the wet concrete. You might not recognise their names, but it shows how big Hong Kong's film industry is. The experience is targeted at tourists from mainland China and the piped music gives it a slightly cheesy feel, but the statue of film legend Bruce Lee pro

items.title: Sik Sik Yuen Wong Tai Sin Temple
items.desc: Next to Wong Tai Sin MTR Station, this is the most popular Taoist temple in Hong Kong. This is where many people ask for divine guidance by a practice known as ''kau cim'' (求籤), a practice that has all but disappeared in mainland China. Entrance is free, though voluntary donations are welcome.

items.title: Shek Kip Mei Estate
items.desc: Built in the 1950s, this is one of the few remaining places where you can grasp the living conditions of Hong Kong during the 50s and 60s. Despite the march of progress promulgated by the Urban Renewal Authority, there are still a few blocks of flats remaining from the 1950s, which are still occupied. Walk from Shek Ki

items.title: Dialogue in the Dark
items.desc: An exhibition in complete darkness. Experience five different Hong Kong themed environments using your non-visual senses with the help of a visually impaired guide. Reservations are recommended.

items.title: Hong Kong Cultural Centre
items.desc: Opened in 1989 and in a prominent position on the waterfront, it is a contender for being the most famous ugly building in Hong Kong. However, if you are a lover of the arts, don't judge this building by its bland exterior; inside the architects have created a superb space that really does justice to the sights and sou

items.title: Hong Kong Museum of Art
items.desc: A fascinating, strange and elusive place. The entrance lies up one floor, mimicking the “temple” approach to the high altar of culture and art. Once you arrive on the first floor, you are bathed in light from the wall of glass that gives you a panoramic view of Hong Kong Island. The objects on show are Chinese ceramics

items.desc: The permanent exhibition, the [http://hk.history.museum/en_US/web/mh/exhibition/permanent.html Hong Kong Story], covers the history of Hong Kong from millions of years ago until the reunification with China in 1997.
